story: Zhenpeng Qiu was last author of a 2026 study on kidney damage caused by tacrolimus, a drug that suppresses the immune system after transplants. The team found that astragaloside IV, a plant compound, protected the kidney in this preclinical work by switching off mTOR. With mTOR off, the protein TFEB became active and the cells could clear damaged material again (autophagy). The study had no human data. PubMed lists Qiu at the School of Pharmacy, Hubei University of Chinese Medicine in Wuhan.

highlights.GAO2026: Last author of the study showing that astragaloside IV protects against tacrolimus kidney damage through the mTOR-TFEB route.

pubmed_affiliation: School of Pharmacy, Hubei University of Chinese Medicine, Wuhan 430065, China.

studies.title: Astragaloside IV Mitigates Tacrolimus-Induced Chronic Nephrotoxicity by Regulating the mTOR-TFEB-GADD45α Pathway.
studies.journal: Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry
studies.finding: Astragaloside IV protects against tacrolimus-induced nephrotoxicity by inhibiting mTOR to activate TFEB and restore autophagy, nominating the mTOR-TFEB-GADD45alpha axis as a calcineurin-independent candidate therapeutic target (preclinical; no human data) in TICN.

current.lab_name: Section Systems Medicine of Metabolism and Signaling, Department of Pediatrics, University Medical Center Groningen, University of Groningen (Groningen, Netherlands)

story: Two studies in the Atlas list Alexander M Heberle as a co-author in the middle of the author list. The 2016 study, done in cells, found that adding amino acids back to starved cells switched on AMPK and mTOR at the same time, so the two are not simple opposites in the first minutes after feeding.
The 2021 study, also in cells, found that G3BP1 and G3BP2 hold the TSC complex on the lysosome and so restrain mTORC1. PubMed lists him at the University Medical Center Groningen in both papers.

highlights.DAL2016: Middle author of the systems study showing that amino acids activate AMPK and mTOR together.
highlights.PRE2021: Middle author of the cell study showing that G3BP proteins tether the TSC complex to lysosomes.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Pediatrics, Section Systems Medicine of Metabolism and Signaling, University of Groningen, University Medical Center Groningen, Groningen 9700 RB, The Netherlands.

studies.title: A systems study reveals concurrent activation of AMPK and mTOR by amino acids
studies.finding: Adding amino acids back to starved cells switched on AMPK, PI3K and mTORC2 acutely and independently of mTORC1, at the same time as mTOR. AMPK activation ran through CaMKK-beta and, under amino acid sufficiency, AMPK kept autophagy going via ULK1. So the textbook picture of AMPK and mTORC1 as simple opposites does not hold in the first minutes after feeding - which matters for how the AMPK-ULK1 feedback arm behaves over time.

studies.title: G3BPs tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and suppress mTORC1 signaling
studies.finding: Adds a physical brake upstream of mTORC1. G3BP1 and G3BP2, known until then as core stress-granule proteins, also sit on the cytoplasmic face of the lysosome and are what holds the TSC complex there; without them TSC cannot reach its target and mTORC1 becomes over-responsive to amino acids and insulin. Loss of G3BP1 reproduces TSC-like hyperactivity phenotypes: faster mTORC1-driven motility in breast cancer cells, with low G3BP1 correlating with worse patient outcome, and disturbed neuronal development in zebrafish. Relevant to the Atlas because it is a lysosomal tethering step that the canonical Rheb/TSC diagram does not show.

current.lab_name: Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute (Cambridge, England, United Kingdom)
current.role: First author of a 2016 live-imaging study of how fast mTORC1 moves to lysosomes after amino acids are added.
current.sub: Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute (PubMed affiliation, 2016)
story: Maria Manifava was first author of a 2016 eLife paper in the Atlas (MAN2016), from the Babraham Institute in Cambridge. Live imaging of human cells showed mTORC1 reaching lysosomes within about 2 minutes of adding amino acids, peaking by 5 minutes. The signal to its usual targets came later, which suggests mTORC1 visits the lysosome briefly and then acts elsewhere.

highlights.MAN2016: First author; PubMed lists the author in the Signalling Programme at the Babraham Institute.

pubmed_affiliation: Signalling Programme, Babraham Institute, Cambridge, United Kingdom.

studies.title: Dynamics of mTORC1 activation in response to amino acids
studies.finding: Live imaging shows mTORC1 moves to lysosomes within 2 minutes of amino acid addition and peaks by 5 minutes, in step with leucine arriving in lysosomes; phosphorylation of classic mTORC1 targets lags behind, suggesting mTORC1 passes briefly through the lysosome before acting on substrates elsewhere.

current.lab_name: Simmaron Research R&D laboratory (Milwaukee, Wisconsin, USA)
current.role: First author of a 2026 phase-II pilot study of low-dose rapamycin in people with ME/CFS.
current.sub: Simmaron Research · Milwaukee, Wisconsin and Incline Village, Nevada, USA
story: Brooke Gile was first author of a small 2026 pilot study of low-dose rapamycin in people with ME/CFS, a long-term illness marked by severe fatigue. There was no placebo group. Patients who responded to rapamycin showed shifts in purine chemicals in their blood, consistent with lower activity of the enzyme IMP dehydrogenase in blood cells. Lab tests suggested that such purine changes can harm mitochondria and feed inflammation in microglia, but those links were not measured in the patients. PubMed lists Gile at Simmaron Research.

highlights.GIL2026: First author of the pilot study linking rapamycin treatment in ME/CFS to reduced fatigue and changed purine levels.

pubmed_affiliation: Simmaron Research R&D laboratory, Milwaukee, WI, USA.

studies.title: Association of rapamycin treatment with the modulation of purine metabolism, reduced microglial inflammatory responses, improved mitochondrial energy metabolism, and alleviation of fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS subjects: pilot findings from phase-II observational study
studies.finding: In an uncontrolled phase-II pilot (no placebo), low-dose rapamycin was associated with reduced fatigue in ME/CFS. In plasma from responders, purine intermediates shifted, consistent with lower IMP dehydrogenase activity in PBMCs. Lab assays suggest that altered purines can impair mitochondrial metabolism and promote microglial inflammation; these links were not measured in patients.

current.lab_name: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University (Chengdu, Sichuan, China)
current.role: Last author of a 2026 study on SLC7A5, mTOR, autophagy and cisplatin tolerance.
current.sub: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases · West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China
story: In a genome-wide CRISPR screen of cancer cells, blocking mTOR made cells more tolerant to cisplatin by switching on protective autophagy, the opposite of the usual view. The amino acid transporter SLC7A5 sits at the centre of this circuit, and adding leucine made SLC7A5-expressing tumour cells more sensitive to cisplatin. Feng is the last of seven authors, and PubMed lists the West China Hospital of Stomatology at Sichuan University.

highlights.RAO2026: Last of seven authors on the CRISPR screen study of SLC7A5, mTOR-autophagy signalling and cisplatin tolerance.

pubmed_affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Oral Diseases, National Center for Stomatology, National Clinical Research Center for Oral Diseases, Frontier Innovation Center for Dental Medicine Plus, Research Unit of Oral Carcinogenesis and Management, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, West China Hospital of Stomatology, Sichuan University, Chengdu, Sichuan, 610041, China.

studies.title: An SLC7A5-dependent nutrient-sensing circuit overcomes cisplatin tolerance via mTOR-autophagy signaling.
studies.finding: A genome-wide CRISPR screen found that mTOR inhibition promotes cisplatin tolerance by activating cytoprotective autophagy — the opposite of the canonical view. SLC7A5 integrates this mTOR-autophagy axis, and leucine supplementation resensitises SLC7A5-expressing tumour cells to cisplatin.

current.lab_name: Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, New York, USA)
current.role: Middle author on both Pavletich-group mTOR structure papers in Nature, from 2013 and 2017.
current.sub: Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (papers from 2013 and 2017)
story: Hyo J Yang is a middle author of two Atlas structure papers in Nature. YAN2013 solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase and showed that its active site sits in a recess guarded by the FRB domain, which also explains how FKBP12-rapamycin blocks it.

YAN2017 gave cryo-EM structures of mTORC1 and of RHEB-bound mTORC1, showing how RHEB switches the kinase on and how PRAS40 blocks it. PubMed lists Yang at the Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, in both papers.

highlights.YAN2013: Middle author: co-author of the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase.
highlights.YAN2017: Middle author: co-author of the structures of mTORC1 with RHEB and PRAS40.

pubmed_affiliation: Structural Biology Program, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, New York 10065, USA.

studies.title: mTOR kinase structure, mechanism and regulation
studies.finding: Solved the crystal structure of the mTOR kinase itself. Revealed why the active site is so hard to reach - it sits in a deep recess guarded by the FRB domain, which acts as a 'gatekeeper' letting substrates in. This structure explains at the atomic level exactly how FKBP12-rapamycin blocks access, and why activating cancer mutations cluster where they do.

studies.title: Mechanisms of mTORC1 activation by RHEB and inhibition by PRAS40
studies.finding: Structures reveal how RHEB allosterically activates and PRAS40 inhibits mTORC1.

current.lab_name: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) (Pozzuoli, Campania, Italy)
current.role: Co-author of the Atlas study SET2012 (lysosome-to-nucleus signaling through mTOR and TFEB).
current.sub: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Pozzuoli, Naples, Italy
story: Diego L Medina is a middle author of a 2012 paper that studied how the lysosome, the cell's recycling compartment, tells the nucleus what it needs. In cells, mTORC1 on the lysosome surface adds a phosphate to the transcription factor TFEB and keeps it inactive. When mTORC1 is blocked, or when the cell is starved or the lysosome is stressed, TFEB moves into the nucleus and turns on lysosome and autophagy genes.

PubMed gives no affiliation for him in this record. The Telethon Institute (TIGEM) comes from two related papers from the same group, where PubMed lists him there and where co-authors of this study also appear.

highlights.SET2012: Middle author of the paper on the lysosome-to-nucleus mTOR and TFEB mechanism.

pubmed_affiliation: Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM), Pozzuoli, Naples, Italy.

studies.title: A lysosome-to-nucleus signalling mechanism senses and regulates the lysosome via mTOR and TFEB
studies.finding: A lysosome-to-nucleus mechanism uses mTOR-dependent TFEB phosphorylation to sense lysosomal state.

current.role: First author of a 2025 review of clinical evidence for off-label rapamycin in healthy adults.
current.sub: The George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences · Washington, DC, USA
story: This 2025 review looks at human evidence for low-dose rapamycin and related drugs in healthy adults, and re-models one cohort with the PhenoAge biological-age clock. Its conclusion is cautious: animal lifespan data are strong, but human data have not yet shown that rapamycin delays aging in healthy people.
Jacob Hands is first author. PubMed lists him at The George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences.

pubmed_affiliation: The George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, Washington DC, DC 20037, USA.

studies.title: What is the clinical evidence to support off-label rapamycin therapy in healthy adults?
studies.finding: A deliberately cautious review of low-dose rapamycin in healthy adults, and re-models one cohort using the PhenoAge biological-aging clock. Verdict: despite strong animal lifespan data, human evidence does NOT yet prove rapamycin delays aging in healthy people. A valuable counterweight to longevity-community hype - it holds the human evidence to a strict standard rather than over-reading promising signals.

current.lab_name: The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine, USA)
current.role: Co-author of 5 Interventions Testing Program mouse lifespan papers in the Atlas.
current.sub: The Jackson Laboratory · Bar Harbor, Maine, USA
story: In the Atlas, Clinton Astle is a middle author on 5 papers from the National Institute on Aging Interventions Testing Program, which tests whether drugs lengthen life in genetically mixed mice at three sites. Together they show that rapamycin extended lifespan in mice, with a bigger effect in females and at higher doses, that acarbose helped mainly males, and that resveratrol, simvastatin and several other popular compounds did not change lifespan. All of this is mouse work.
PubMed lists no affiliation for Clinton Astle in these records. A 2016 paper from the same program, sharing several co-authors, lists him at The Jackson Laboratory in Bar Harbor, Maine.

highlights.MIL2011: Middle author of the program paper in which rapamycin extended lifespan but resveratrol and simvastatin did not.
highlights.MIL2014: Middle author of the program paper showing rapamycin lifespan extension depends on dose and sex.

pubmed_affiliation: The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME, USA.

studies.title: Evaluation of resveratrol, green tea extract, curcumin, oxaloacetic acid, and medium-chain triglyceride oil on life span of genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
studies.finding: None of five popular longevity compounds had a statistically significant effect on lifespan. The paper explicitly states the ITP's mission is to publish all results, positive or negative - the exact registry model this Atlas should emulate.

studies.title: Acarbose, 17-α-estradiol, and nordihydroguaiaretic acid extend mouse lifespan preferentially in males.
studies.finding: Beyond rapamycin, the same ITP program found acarbose extended male median lifespan by 22% - evidence that the registry surfaces real positive hits too, not only negative results.

studies.title: Rapamycin, but not resveratrol or simvastatin, extends life span of genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
studies.finding: In the same experimental design that showed rapamycin extended median lifespan by 10-18%, neither resveratrol nor simvastatin had any significant effect on survival - a direct head-to-head negative control run at the same time, in the same mice.

studies.title: Rapamycin-mediated lifespan increase in mice is dose and sex dependent and metabolically distinct from dietary restriction
studies.finding: Rapamycin's lifespan extension in mice is dose-dependent and greater in females.

studies.title: Rapamycin fed late in life extends lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice
studies.finding: Rapamycin fed from 600 days of age extended median and maximal lifespan in both sexes; age at 90% mortality rose 14% in females and 9% in males.

current.lab_name: The Sam and Ann Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
current.role: First author of the 2018 study of long-term rapamycin and blood markers in middle-aged marmosets.
current.sub: Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio
story: Aubrey M. Sills was first author of a 2018 paper in the Atlas, with Adam B. Salmon as last author. PubMed lists the author at the Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies at UT Health San Antonio.

Middle-aged common marmosets got daily rapamycin. After nine months their blood cell counts changed only a little. Females had lower rapamycin levels in blood than males, yet both sexes changed little, so blood side effects look unlikely in healthy middle-aged animals of this kind.

highlights.SIL2018: First author of the marmoset study of long-term rapamycin and hematological markers.

pubmed_affiliation: The Sam and Ann Barshop Institute for Longevity and Aging Studies, UT Health San Antonio, San Antonio, Texas

studies.title: Long-term treatment with the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin has minor effect on clinical laboratory markers in middle-aged marmosets.
studies.finding:
In middle-aged marmosets given daily rapamycin, 9 months of treatment produced only minor changes in cellular blood counts, so hematological side effects are not likely outcomes of long-term rapamycin in relatively healthy middle-aged animals. Trough blood concentrations of rapamycin were significantly lower in females than in males, yet both sexes changed little. At baseline, males and females differed little in morphology or in markers of blood cell counts, metabolism and inflammation.
Boundary: healthy middle-aged marmosets, 9 months, hematology and clinical laboratory markers only; it says nothing about efficacy or lifespan, and the abstract does not give the dose or group sizes.

story: The EXIST-3 trial gave everolimus or placebo to 366 people with tuberous sclerosis complex whose focal seizures had not responded to standard drugs. According to PubMed, about 15% of the placebo group had their seizures cut by half or more, against 28% on low-dose and 40% on high-dose everolimus. This was a randomised, double-blind trial in people.

Paolo Curatolo is a middle author on the paper, and PubMed lists him at Tor Vergata University Hospital in Rome. The Atlas also has him as a middle author of a second tuberous sclerosis trial, but that record gives no affiliation, so it is not included here.

highlights.FRE2016: Middle author of the phase 3 EXIST-3 trial, listed at Tor Vergata University Hospital, Rome.

pubmed_affiliation: Tor Vergata University Hospital, Rome, Italy.

studies.title: Adjunctive everolimus therapy for treatment-resistant focal-onset seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis (EXIST-3): a phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study
studies.finding: EXIST-3 was a phase 3, double-blind trial in 366 patients aged 2 to 65 with tuberous sclerosis complex and focal seizures that had not responded to standard drugs. They were randomised 1:1:1 to placebo (n=119), everolimus dosed to a low blood trough of 3-7 ng/mL (n=117) or a high trough of 9-15 ng/mL (n=130), added to their existing antiepileptic drugs. story: Julie A. Mattison is first author of an Atlas study (MAT2017) that compared two long-running caloric restriction studies in rhesus monkeys, one at the National Institute on Aging and one at the University of Wisconsin. Putting the data side by side, the authors found health benefits from eating less in both, and saw that survival results depended on study design and on what the control animals ate.

She is also a co-author of the 2021 marmoset paper (HOR2021), which built epigenetic age clocks and found no significant effect of rapamycin on them. In both papers PubMed lists her at the Translational Gerontology Branch of the National Institute on Aging.

studies.title: DNA methylation age analysis of rapamycin in common marmosets.
studies.finding:
The authors built two epigenetic clocks for common marmoset blood from DNA methylation data; the human-marmoset clock for relative age correlated moderately well with age in vervet monkeys and rhesus macaques. In a separate marmoset cohort they tested whether rapamycin would change epigenetic age. The clocks did not detect a significant effect of rapamycin on the epigenetic age of marmoset blood.
Boundary: a null result on one biomarker (DNA methylation age in blood). It does not show that rapamycin has no effect on aging in marmosets, only that these clocks did not register one; the abstract gives no dose, duration or group size.

José Guerrero-Morín is first author. PubMed lists him at the Monterrey unit of Cinvestav in Mexico.

studies.title: Crosstalk dynamics between the circadian clock and the mTORC1 pathway
studies.finding: A mathematical model of how mTORC1 could tune the circadian clock. It suggests mTORC1 raises clock amplitude by controlling BMAL1 translation and shortens the period by controlling where BMAL1 sits in the cell, and that both levels are needed for robust oscillation. A model, not a measurement - it proposes mechanisms for RAM2018's observations rather than testing them.

current.role: First author of a 2012 mouse study showing that rapamycin slows several aspects of aging.
current.sub: Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine & Department of Pathology, University of Michigan · Ann Arbor, MI, USA
story: This 2012 mouse study asked whether rapamycin only prevents the cancers that kill mice, or slows aging more widely. Age-related changes in heart, liver, adrenal glands, endometrium and tendon, and the decline in spontaneous activity, all came on more slowly in treated mice. The mice also had more testicular degeneration and cataracts.

John Wilkinson is first author. PubMed lists him at the Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Department of Pathology, University of Michigan. Three other Atlas records use the name form J Erby Wilkinson without an affiliation, so they are not included.

highlights.WIL2012: First author of the rapamycin and aging paper.

pubmed_affiliation: Unit for Laboratory Animal Medicine and Department of Pathology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, USA.

studies.title: Rapamycin slows aging in mice
studies.finding: Answered a crucial objection: does rapamycin really slow AGING, or just prevent the cancers that kill mice? By showing slower age-related change across many tissues (heart, liver, tendon, activity), it argued for genuine slowing of aging. Honestly reported harms too - more cataracts and testicular degeneration - making it a balanced landmark, not hype.

story: Giancarlo Maruri Munaretto was last author of the Atlas study VITTE2026 in JHLT Open, a meta-analysis of 60 studies with 1786 heart transplant recipients. Everolimus-based treatment slowed cardiac allograft vasculopathy on ultrasound and kept kidney function better when the dose of calcineurin inhibitors was lowered. Death rates were about the same, while side effects and stopping of treatment were more common. PubMed lists Munaretto at the Universidade do Contestado in Santa Catarina, Brazil.

studies.title: Efficacy and safety of everolimus in heart transplant recipients: A meta-analysis
studies.finding: Meta-analysis of 60 studies (1786 heart transplant recipients): everolimus-based immunosuppression reduced cardiac allograft vasculopathy progression on IVUS (RR ~0.57) and preserved renal function (eGFR +10-15 mL/min) when combined with calcineurin-inhibitor minimisation, with neutral all-cause mortality (RR ~0.98) but more adverse events and treatment discontinuation.

story: James C. Yao was first author of the Atlas study YAO2011 in the New England Journal of Medicine, the RADIANT-3 trial. It randomized 410 patients with advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours to everolimus or placebo. Median progression-free survival was 11.0 months with everolimus and 4.6 months with placebo, and side effects were mostly mild. PubMed lists Yao at the M.D. Anderson Cancer Center in Houston.

studies.title: Everolimus for advanced pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (RADIANT-3)
studies.finding: A phase 3 RCT (n=410) that made everolimus a standard treatment for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. It more than doubled progression-free survival (11.0 vs 4.6 months, a 65% reduction in risk of progression/death) with mostly mild side effects. Another FDA-approved indication built on blocking mTOR.

current.sub: Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research, Cambridge, MA · listed on four Atlas papers, 2014–2021
story: Jose M Orozco is a co-author on four papers in the Atlas, all listed at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts, between 2014 and 2021. PubMed shows the Whitehead Institute together with the Massachusetts Institute of Technology on the earlier papers. He is third author on the 2014 paper and a middle author on the others.

The papers cover how mTORC1 learns about its surroundings. Sestrins bind GATOR2 to dampen amino-acid signalling (2014). KICSTOR holds GATOR1 at the lysosome so nutrients can regulate mTORC1 (2017). SAMTOR senses S-adenosylmethionine, a methyl donor linked to methionine (2017). Genome-wide CRISPR screens showed that AMPK and HRI relay mitochondrial dysfunction to mTORC1 (2021). All four are cell studies.

story: Two Atlas studies list Kivanç Birsoy as a middle author. One catalogued cancer-linked MTOR mutations, found 33 that switch the pathway on, and showed that cancer cells carrying them were more sensitive to rapamycin in cell culture and in mouse xenografts. The other, in mice, found that calorie restriction lowers mTORC1 activity in Paneth cells of the gut and that this boosts the intestinal stem cells next to them.

PubMed lists no affiliation for him in either record. A 2012 paper on which he is first author shares four co-authors with these studies and places him at the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

studies.title: mTORC1 in the Paneth cell niche couples intestinal stem-cell function to calorie intake
studies.finding: Mice kept on calorie restriction (60% of normal intake) had more intestinal stem cells and Paneth cells, the cells that form the stem-cell niche (Lgr5+ stem cells 5.6% vs 4.3% of crypt cells, Paneth cells 9.8% vs 6.7%), and their crypts were nearly twice as likely to form organoids. In co-culture, Paneth cells from restricted mice, not stem cells, carried the boost. Restriction lowered S6 and S6K1 phosphorylation in crypts, and feeding or insulin switched on mTORC1 in Paneth cells but not in stem cells; forcing mTORC1 back on during restriction (Rheb induction or Tsc1 deletion) cancelled the effect, while one week of rapamycin copied it and did not add to restriction.
